lead.title: Google gives AI a multiple-choice test and asks it to stop writing essays
lead.summary: Google introduced Gemini Decisions API, a service for structured, closed-set judgments such as classifying an image or scoring answers against a rubric. Google's announcement says it can process up to 1,000 questions in one request across text, images, audio, video and PDFs. This is a product announcement and Google's own description of its capabilities, not independent performance validation.
lead.whyCare: For workflows that need labels or decisions at scale, a purpose-built endpoint may be easier to evaluate than asking a general chatbot to explain itself 1,000 times.

news.title: The AI market’s Jensen-shaped question mark
news.summary: Axios and the Associated Press report that Nvidia leadership questions and concerns around the wider AI investment boom are weighing on AI-related stocks. The coverage describes developing corporate and market uncertainty; it does not establish a final board decision about CEO Jensen Huang.
news.whyCare: AI's supply chain and investor confidence are concentrated around a small number of firms. Leadership risk can move markets before it changes a model roadmap.

news.title: The paper pile grows; evaluation gets a useful reality check
news.summary: Today's roundup highlights research on compute-matched evaluation, sparse model edits, and coding-agent benchmarks. One useful lesson across the papers: a method that wins per training step may lose when compared at equal compute. These are preprint claims summarized by a third-party digest, not settled findings.
news.whyCare: When comparing AI research, ask whether methods were tested with the same compute budget. A win per training step can disappear when the full cost is counted.

learning.title: Closed-set decisions
learning.body: A closed-set decision model chooses among options you define ahead of time—say, “invoice valid / invalid / needs review”—instead of generating an open-ended answer. This makes outputs easier to validate and can make repetitive classification cheaper. It also means the model cannot give a good answer if the right option is missing or the question itself is ambiguous.
learning.tryThis: Take ten recent support requests. Write a small fixed label set, then ask a model to assign each request a label plus confidence. Count human disagreements and cases where the right label was missing.

focus.text: If you run high-volume classification, compare a structured decision endpoint with your current prompt on a small, human-reviewed sample before changing production.
Look for primary confirmation of any Nvidia board or leadership decision; early market coverage is not a resolved corporate event.
Don’t infer broad AI capability from a leaderboard number or roundup blurb. Read the evaluation setup.
